messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: In the univariate analysis, vitamin D levels showed no significant association with depression or other geriatric assessment variables, apart from hypertension.
Sentence: "In univariate analysis, no significant associations were found between vitamin D and other variables, except for hypertension (p = 0.049)."
Measured as: depression (geriatric assessment)
Population: Elderly individuals aged 65-100 years receiving home healthcare services
Intervention: Serum vitamin D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Vitamin D categories (severe deficiency, deficiency, other groups)
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 439
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Higher serum 25(OH)D was correlated with lower depressive symptom scores (GDS) across participants.
Sentence: "Serum 25(OH)D correlated positively with MoCA and MMSE scores and inversely with ADL, IADL, and GDS scores."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (GDS)
Population: Hospitalised adults aged 65 or older admitted for comprehensive geriatric assessment in Cluj-Napoca, Romania
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D level (measured, not given)
Comparator: Lower serum 25(OH)D levels
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 1,438
baseline_vitamin_d_status: mixed

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are cross-sectional associations of serum vitamin D with geriatric depression scores, but Study A reports no significant univariate association while Study B reports an inverse correlation with GDS, differing mainly in population (home-healthcare elderly vs hospitalised adults) and sample size.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["design_or_bias"],"detail":"population: home healthcare recipients aged 65-100 vs hospitalised adults aged 65+; Study A's null is univariate only, with n = 439 vs 1,438"}
